c.tagline: A Red Sea dive capital on the Sinai Peninsula's tip, with coral walls just offshore from all-inclusive resorts

card: Widely accepted at hotels and larger restaurants; cash useful for the Old Market and taxis

taxi.fare: Negotiated flat rate, as meters are uncommon
taxi.fareNote: Agree the fare before departure; hotel-arranged transfers are common and reliable

emergency.note: Tourist police (180) can assist with English-language support

english.label: Easy to get by in English

walk: Naama Bay and the resort strip are walkable; the Old Market and other neighborhoods require a taxi

safety.safety: Generally safe in the resort areas, with a strong tourist police presence; check current travel advisories for the wider Sinai region
safety.crime: Petty theft and overcharging by unlicensed vendors are the main practical concerns

hood_landmark.Naama Bay: Naama Bay's beachfront promenade of hotels and restaurants
hood_landmark.Old Market (Sharm El Maya): The Old Market's Bedouin crafts and traditional cafes
hood_landmark.Hadaba: Hadaba's clifftop resort hotels overlooking the bay
hood_landmark.Nabq Bay: Nabq Bay's quieter northern resort strip

avoid.reason: Avoid overland travel into central and northern Sinai beyond the resort corridor, which most governments advise against due to terrorism risk.
Expect persistent touts in Naama Bay and taxi overcharging — agree prices upfront and choose reputable dive operators.

hood_desc: The lively main resort strip with the highest concentration of hotels, restaurants, dive shops, and nightlife.
The original town center with traditional souks, spice shops, and a more authentically Egyptian atmosphere.
A clifftop area of upscale resorts with panoramic Red Sea views, a short drive from Naama Bay's action.
A quieter, more family-oriented resort area north of the main strip, popular for calmer beaches.

A run of large beachfront resorts on the coast between Naama Bay and Ras Nasrani, wrapped around a bay whose house reef drops away straight off the shore. Self-contained and quiet after dark, it suits divers and families more than bar-hoppers.
lodging: Renaissance Sharm El Sheikh Golden View Beach Resort
Rehana Sharm Resort Aqua Park & Spa
Four Seasons Resort Sharm El Sheikh

water.note: Drink bottled water only, including for brushing teeth.

transit.sys: No formal municipal bus network; hotel shuttles and taxis are the norm
transit.hours: Taxis run around the clock in resort areas
transit.map: Not centrally published; hotels arrange transport and excursions
transit.note: Most visitors book excursions and airport transfers through their hotel or a tour operator

transport.air: Sharm El Sheikh International Airport (SSH), about 15-20 min from Naama Bay
transport.train: No passenger rail service to Sharm El Sheikh
transport.bus: Long-distance buses connect to Cairo and other Egyptian cities (long journey)
transport.car: Rental cars are available but most visitors rely on taxis and hotel transfers

net.w: Free wifi standard in hotels and cafes
net.ops: Vodafone Egypt, Orange Egypt, Etisalat Misr
net.fwn: Free wifi widely available in hotels
net.ap: A Vodafone or Orange Egypt tourist SIM or eSIM

tip.s: 10-15% is customary for dive guides and tour operators
tip.r: 10% is standard, though often added automatically at resort restaurants

food.name: Grilled Red Sea fish
food.desc: Whole sea bream, bass or hammour salted and charcoal-grilled, sold by weight with tahina, salads and warm baladi bread.

places.name: Fares Seafood
places.note: Open since 1994 and always full of locals; order by weight from the ice counter.

places.name: El Fanar
places.note: Seafront tables under the lighthouse; grilled catch with a view over the reef.

food.name: Seafood tagen
food.desc: Calamari and prawns baked in a clay pot with tomato, garlic, cumin and chilli until thick and bubbling; eaten with bread, not cutlery.

places.name: Fares Seafood
places.note: The mixed calamari and shrimp tagen is the dish regulars order every time.

places.name: Old Market fish restaurants
places.note: A whole street of grills; compare ice counters before sitting down.

food.name: Koshari
food.desc: Rice, lentils and pasta piled together with spiced tomato sauce, chickpeas and fried onions, sharpened with garlic vinegar and chilli.

places.name: El Masrab
places.note: Cosy Egyptian kitchen doing mezze and a well-made koshari away from resort menus.

places.name: Al-Aswani Restaurant
places.note: Broad Egyptian menu; koshari, fatta, foul and grills in one place.

food.name: Sayadeya
food.desc: Sinai-style fish baked into rice cooked in spiced tomato and onion stock, often finished with toasted nuts; the local celebration plate.

places.name: Fares Seafood
places.note: Second branch away from the market, same kitchen and same fish counter.

places.name: El Masrab
places.note: Home-style Egyptian cooking; ask what the kitchen has cooked that day.

food.name: Taameya and mezze
food.desc: Fava-bean falafel fried green and crisp, eaten with hummus, baba ghanoush, tahina and pickles as the standard Egyptian starter spread.

places.name: L'Orient Restaurant
places.note: Known locally for its shawarma and falafel; quick, cheap and consistently good.

places.name: Al-Aswani Restaurant
places.note: Big mezze selection: hummus, fattoush, mutabal and freshly fried taameya.

food.name: Om Ali
food.desc: Egypt's warm bread pudding: pastry soaked in sweetened milk with nuts, coconut and raisins, baked until the top blisters golden.

places.name: El Masrab
places.note: Served hot from the oven; the usual way to end an Egyptian meal here.

places.name: Old Market sweet shops
places.note: Om Ali, basbousa and konafa by the portion, alongside the spice and tea stalls.

food.name: Shai bil naana
food.desc: Black tea boiled strong and poured over fresh mint with plenty of sugar; the ahwa ritual that follows every meal and every shisha.

places.name: Farsha Cafe
places.note: Cushioned cliffside terraces above the sea; mint tea and shisha at sunset.

places.name: Old Market tea houses
places.note: Traditional ahwas beside the spice stalls; also good Turkish coffee.

food.name: Karkade
food.desc: Hibiscus flowers steeped into a tart crimson tea, served iced through the day and hot in the evening; caffeine-free and everywhere.

places.name: Old Market tea houses
places.note: Cheapest and most authentic; the stalls also sell dried hibiscus to take home.

places.name: Farsha Cafe
places.note: Iced karkade and fresh juices with the best sea view in Sharm.

landmarks: Ras Mohammed National Park
Egypt's premier marine park at the Sinai Peninsula's tip, where sheer coral walls, shark reefs and turquoise lagoons draw divers worldwide.
Naama Bay
Sharm's palm-lined heart, a crescent of beach clubs, promenade cafés and neon nightlife wrapped around a calm, swimmable bay.
Al Sahaba Mosque
A striking modern mosque in the Old Market blending Ottoman, Fatimid and Mamluk styles, its ornate minarets glowing beautifully at night.
Old Market (Sharm El Maya)
The town's traditional souk quarter, buzzing with spice stalls, shisha cafés and bargain-friendly bazaars a world away from the resorts.
Ras Um Sid
A lighthouse-topped headland with one of Sharm's best house reefs, where a coral drop-off teems with fish just steps from shore.
Strait of Tiran Reefs
Four legendary offshore reefs, Jackson, Woodhouse, Thomas and Gordon, swept by currents that bring big pelagics to snorkellers and divers by boat.
SOHO Square
A glitzy entertainment plaza of fountains, restaurants and an ice bar in Sharks Bay, the resort city's favourite evening playground.
The Heavenly Cathedral (El Sama-a Cathedral)
A Coptic Orthodox church whose vividly painted ceiling frescoes of biblical scenes rank it among Egypt's most beautiful modern churches.
St. Catherine's Monastery
A UNESCO-listed 6th-century Greek Orthodox monastery at the foot of Mount Sinai, guarding ancient icons and the Burning Bush, a classic day trip.
Mount Sinai (Jebel Musa)
The revered 2,285-metre peak where Moses is said to have received the Ten Commandments, climbed at dawn for an unforgettable desert sunrise.

train.note: There is no railway in Sinai - Egyptian National Railways does not extend beyond the Suez Canal on this side. All travel is by road or air, and Sharm El Sheikh International Airport has direct flights from across Europe and the Gulf.

bus.note: No scheduled international coaches; the Israeli border at Taba is crossed on foot with a change of vehicle. Go Bus (https://go-bus.com/) and East Delta Travel run from the Sharm terminal to Cairo in about 7-8 hours and to Dahab in 90 minutes and Nuweiba for the Jordan ferry. Book Go Bus online. Check current travel advice for overland Sinai routes.

intl.to: Hurghada (Egypt) - across the Gulf of Suez, service intermittent
intl.op: Red Sea fast-ferry operators — check current status locally

ferry.note: There is no international ferry from Sharm El Sheikh itself - the crossing to Aqaba in Jordan sails from Nuweiba, about three hours north. The cross-gulf catamaran to Hurghada has started and stopped repeatedly over the years, so confirm locally before relying on it. Boats from the marina at Naama Bay are dive and snorkel trips to Ras Mohammed and Tiran.

half.name: Dahab
half.blurb: A laid-back Red Sea diving town with the famous Blue Hole sinkhole and a relaxed lagoon-side promenade.

half.name: Nabq Protected Area
half.blurb: A coastal reserve north of the city with mangrove stands, a fossilized coral reef, and Bedouin-run beach camps.

full.name: Colored Canyon
full.blurb: A narrow sandstone slot canyon near Nuweiba with striated red, purple, and yellow rock walls, explored on foot.
